newsitem.title: USA: CBOT board votes to end night pit trade, extend day. [CORRECTED 1:30 GMT 17/4]
newsitem.headline: CBOT board votes to end night pit trade, extend day. [CORRECTED 1:30 GMT 17/4]

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Wednesday said its directors approved a plan to end the exchange's 10-year-old evening open outcry session and to extend the daytime pit session by one hour until 1500 local time.
If members approve the plan, the changes would become effective the first week of April 1998, said Frederick Grede, CBOT executive vice president.
The proposal must now be put to a full membership vote. A date for the vote has not yet been set, Grede said.
The board's decision to end night pit trading came after considerable debate among board members that ultimately boiled down to the issue of competitiveness, Grede said.
"Obviously, the reason is from a pure business perspective, to try to maximize the business of the Chicago Board of Trade," Grede said.
In opting to expand the daytime pit session, the board took into consideration the later closing times for the cash Treasury market and other competing markets, Grede said.

The move to end the night session follows several years of mushrooming growth for Project A, the CBOT's after-hours electronic system, and a seemingly irreversible slide in evening pit trading volume.

Under the new plan, Project A trading will start at 4 p.m. Central time (2100 GMT during daylight savings time and 2200 GMT during standard time), two hours after the current afternoon Project A session begins.

CBOT financial products, including the benchmark Treasury bond futures contract, currently trade via open outcry during evening hours from 1820 to 2105 Central time. The night session follows two hours of late-afternoon electronic trading and precedes the overnight Project A session.

Daily night trading volume averaged 8,000 contracts in March, down from peak volume of 18,000 contracts in 1990, according to exchange figures. By contrast, an average 21,000 contracts a day traded on Project A last month, nearly a 10-fold increase in two years.

The debate over night trading pitted powerful futures commission merchants, who have come to bemoan the session as a financial drain, against local traders and others who see it as an important training ground for young talent and a service to overseas customers, the primary market for which it was created.
